Figure 9-47 shows the code for a new GUI application that a programmer started simply by dragging Button onto a Form. If you click on Form1.Designer.cs in the Solution Explorer and scroll down, you can display the code where the Button is declared. See Figure 9-47.

![](bbox=[0.137, 0.175, 0.862, 0.608])

**Figure 9-47** The automatically generated statement that declares button1

If you right-click button1 in the code and select Find References from the menu that appears, a list of every reference to button1 in the project is displayed in the Find Symbol Results area at the bottom of the IDE (You might need to resize the window to see the references clearly.). You can double-click each entry in the list to locate all the places where code has been generated for button1. For example, several instances of button1 are in a method named InitializeComponent(), as shown in Figure 9-4. The first reference to button1 calls its constructor. You can also see how the Button's Name, Location, Size, and other properties are set. You could have written these statements, especially when you know more about objects and how they are constructed, but it is easier to develop an application by dragging a Button onto a Form and letting the IDE create these statements for you.
